thread.title: UPDATE: Why Apple should have marketed the iPhone X like a gourmet jam

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Why Apple should have marketed the iPhone X like a gourmet jam

organizations.name: stern school of business at new york university

text:
By Alessandra Malito, MarketWatch
Consumers were baffled by the tech giant's usually stellar marketing tactics
Apple(AAPL)is reportedly slowing production of the iPhone X after lower-than-anticipated demand (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-stock-drops-after-report-of-iphone-x-production-cut-2018-01-29), and we're all left to wonder: What went wrong?
The iPhone X was supposed to mark the iconic smartphone's 10th anniversary. Instead, Apple is cutting production from 40 million units to 20 million iPhone X handsets in the first quarter, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal (https://www.wsj.com/articles/apple-to-curtail-iphone-x-production-in-the-face-of-weak-demand-1517312098), which cited a person described as knowledgeable about Apple's production goals.
Apple is usually a leader in branding and messaging, but this time it stumbled, said Tom Meyvis, professor of marketing and coordinator of the Ph.D. program in marketing at the Stern School of Business at New York University. Consumers were faced with too many iPhones being released at the same time, and too many variations of the iPhone X, he said. "Consumers eventually adapt to everything, even continuous improvements," Meyvis said.
Shoppers are dazzled by too many choices
A now-famous study (https://faculty.washington.edu/jdb/345/345%20Articles/Iyengar%20%26%20Lepper%20(2000).pdf) in 2000 by psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper presented consumers in an upmarket store with 23 varieties of jam on one day and just six varieties of jam on another day. Those who sampled the jam were given a dollar off the marked price. Even though more people tried jam at the bigger table, only 3% of people bought jam from that table, while 30% bought jam from the table with fewer items.
Apple fans know the iPhone will make their life easier, and they trust the product will fulfill their expectations. But they're exhausted by so much choice. "Apple customers are not necessarily looking for a specific product to fulfill a specific need," Meyvis said. "They are simply looking to upgrade."
A 2015 study published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology, among others, supports that 2000 jam experiment and the so-called paradox of choice. That study (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1057740814000916?np=y) identified four key factors -- complexity of choice, decision-making difficulties, preference uncertainty and decision goals -- that can lead to choice overload. "We further show that each of these four factors has a reliable and significant impact," it said.
See: Warren Buffett prefers flip phones -- and he's not alone (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/move-over-iphone-x-some-people-prefer-an-old-fashioned-flip-phone-2017-09-12)
Apple's marketing problems with the iPhone X were complex
Apple had other issues making it more difficult for consumers to choose the iPhone X. The iPhone X came out in November 2017, only two months after the Cupertino, Calif.--based tech giant released the iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus. Many people didn't know what to call the iPhone X when it first came out. (It's pronounced "10" rather than "X" in honor of the product line's anniversary.)
And they were compounded by trust issues. At the same time as the phone's release, Apple was in the middle of a scandal, with customers criticizing the company for purposefully slowing down iPhones with older batteries to avoid them shutting down. Apple later apologized and dropped the price of replacement batteries from $79 to $29 (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-iphone-x-got-upstaged-by-apples-battery-scandal-2018-01-05).
Of course, it's easier to taste a different jam than figure out how a $1,000 iPhone X is different from the last. The phone has flashy new features, like facial recognition and wireless charging, but experts say the company may be pushing its luck (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/has-apple-lost-the-plot-with-the-1000-iphone-x-2017-11-02) by asking customers to spend so much.
Apple, famously, has a community of loyal fans, and it's expanding, said Barbara Kahn, professor of marketing at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. People often go to Apple's stores just to try the products and hang out. "When I'm walking around malls, the Apple store is still the most crowded," she said. "People are waiting outside on line for the Apple store to open."
-Alessandra Malito;
